overview: This file assembles U.S. diplomatic and consular records concerning the censorship, opening, damage, and detention of foreign mail by Japanese military, postal, or other authorities, principally during 1938–1939. It includes cross-reference sheets for reports from Shanghai, China, Tianjin, Qingdao, and Batavia; a detailed Tianjin despatch with postal-service replies concerning damaged correspondence and censored copies of Reader’s Digest; and an embassy despatch documenting an Iranian protest over mail opened in Japan. The final cross-reference concerns mail from China reportedly detained at Shanghai because American President Lines vessels were allegedly barred from carrying it across the Pacific. Several documents expose the tension between officials’ private acknowledgment of Japanese censorship and their unwillingness or inability to admit it formally.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on censorship of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report that official censors opened and read mail sent to or from foreigners in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Shanghai report: all foreigners' mail in Taiwan, especially officials', was opened and read by censors.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference on censorship of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan
subfiles.about: A duplicate sheet records systematic examination of foreigners’ mail in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cross-reference repeating that all foreigners' mail in Taiwan, especially officials', was opened and read by censors.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on examination of official American mail at Harbin
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report concerning the examination of official American mail at Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Tianjin report on official American mail examined at Harbin, filed at 125.4616/70.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Caldwell’s initial report on censorship at Tianjin
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes an initial report on censored American mail and a promise of inquiry by the Japanese Consul General.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Caldwell's despatch No. 612: Consul General Horiuchi promised to investigate censorship of American mail at Tianjin.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Caldwell’s supplementary report on censorship at Tianjin
subfiles.about: The sheet records the absence of official information about tampered mail and a Japanese assurance that complaints would not recur.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Caldwell's follow-up report: Consul Tanaka assured no further cause for complaint over Tianjin mail tampering.

subfiles.title: Caldwell despatch on Japanese military censorship of American mail
subfiles.from: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Beijing
subfiles.about: Caldwell reports privately acknowledged Japanese military interference with American consular mail and encloses three postal replies and a damaged envelope.
subfiles.summary: Caldwell reports Chinese postal officials denied finding where mail was tampered with, though the director privately knew Japanese military censors were responsible but dared not say so; Japan's Consul General didn't deny it and relayed assurances from Beijing military headquarters.

subfiles.title: Caretti letter acknowledging two American postal complaints
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, U.S. Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti acknowledges complaints about irregularities affecting mail addressed to American consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: Caretti reports Caldwell's March 28 mail complaint was referred to the Peiping Road Post Office, and a second complaint is under investigation.

subfiles.title: Caretti reply concerning the opened Chang Fong Mee envelope
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti reports that postal inquiries could not establish responsibility for apparent tampering with an embassy letter.
subfiles.summary: Caretti reports no evidence the opened, resealed envelope to Mrs. Chang Fong Mee was tampered with in postal custody, suggesting mailbag friction instead and returning it.

subfiles.title: Caretti reply concerning censored copies of Reader’s Digest
subfiles.from: E. Caretti, Director of Posts for Hebei pro tempore
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, American Consul General at Tianjin
subfiles.about: Caretti responds to a protest that pages had been removed from magazines addressed to American consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: Caretti reports an investigation couldn't determine why pages were torn from Caldwell's uncensor-stamped April 1938 Reader's Digest copies, noting unregistered mail left no tracking record.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Grew’s Iranian protest despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: An internal review note dismisses the need for action on the Iranian protest over opened diplomatic mail in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Grew's despatch No. 3156 dismisses an Iranian protest over Japanese postal censorship as unsubstantiated and typical of Iranian diplomatic methods, recommending no action.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch transmitting the Iranian protest
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits an Iranian diplomatic protest over an opened letter and compares it with American experience involving mail to Taipei.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards the dean of the diplomatic corps' circular and Iran's protest over opened mail, calling it unsupported, but notes the Embassy showed a wax-sealed cover to Japan's Foreign Office as evidence confidential mail isn't sent ordinarily.

subfiles.title: Bassompierre circular on the Iranian mail complaint
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.to: Members of the Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The dean circulates Sheybany’s protest while declining for the moment to intervene collectively.
subfiles.summary: Bassompierre circulates Iran's protest to Foreign Minister Ugaki, telling colleagues there's no current reason for diplomatic-corps intervention unless further incidents suggest a systematic practice.

subfiles.title: Sheybany protest over opened Iranian diplomatic mail
subfiles.to: General Kazushige Ugaki, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Sheybany formally protests two incidents involving opened mail addressed to the Iranian Legation and threatens reciprocal action.
subfiles.summary: Sheybany protests that an open parcel and now an open registered letter reached Iran's Legation despite Hirota's assurances, demanding an apology, dismissal of the responsible official, and guarantees, threatening reciprocal mail-opening.

subfiles.title: English translation of Bassompierre’s circular note
subfiles.from: Baron de Bassompierre, Dean of the Diplomatic Corps
subfiles.to: Members of the Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The enclosure translates the dean’s French circular concerning the Iranian request for collective diplomatic action.
subfiles.summary: Translation records Bassompierre circulating Sheybany's complaint to Ugaki, declining collective diplomatic-corps representations for now but leaving open future action if violations recur systematically.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on censorship of the American Consulate’s mail at Qingdao
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report and protest concerning Japanese detention of an American consular letter at Qingdao.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Sokobin reported Japanese censorship of the American Consulate's mail at Qingdao and protested the detention of a consular letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese censorship of mail at Batavia
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on Japanese mail censorship accompanied by an envelope that had been opened.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Dickover's report on Japanese mail censorship at Batavia included an opened envelope as physical evidence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on mail from China detained at Shanghai
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an inquiry into reports that U.S.-bound mail was being held at Shanghai because American President Lines vessels could not carry it across the Pacific.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a telegram disputes a press report that the Maritime Commission barred China-U.S. mail on American President Lines ships.

interest: Shows Japanese mail censorship across China and Taiwan, contrasted with official denials and weak evidentiary excuses.
